```{r options, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5.5, fig.align = "center",
                      dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(digits = 3, width = 90)
```

When people work with a generative AI tool over several weeks, the way they
interact with it can change: they may learn which requests the tool handles
well, delegate more, check less, or become more frustrated with its
failures. Whether such a change has occurred is a question about the
process of interaction, not about how often each action occurs, and it is
answered by comparing the transition structure of early and late sessions.
With two actors the comparison has a further layer: the change can lie in
how each actor continues its own turn or in how the actors hand over to
each other.

This case study compares the first and second halves of a set of vibe-coding
sessions, in which programmers directed an AI coding agent. It asks, in
turn, whether the two networks differ at all, in which actor-pair blocks
the differences lie, which individual transitions differ and with what
certainty, and whether the turn-taking patterns between the actors have
changed.

```{r package}
library(htna)
set.seed(2026)
```

## Data

`human_ai` holds the coded turns of 429 vibe-coding sessions. Each row is
one coded event.

- **Session and order:** `session_id`, `order_in_session`; transitions are
  counted within sessions.
- **Code:** `code`, six human codes (`Check`, `Frustrate`, `Inquire`,
  `Refine`, `Request`, `Specify`) and six AI codes (`Ask`, `Delegate`,
  `Execute`, `Plan`, `Repair`, `Report`).
- **Actor type:** `actor_type`, `"Human"` or `"AI"`.
- **Phase:** `phase`, `Early` or `Late`: the sessions ordered by their first
  date and split in half (214 and 215 sessions).

```{r build}
grp <- build_htna(human_ai, actor_type = "actor_type", group = "phase")
grp
```

Both networks contain all twelve codes; the early network has 135 non-zero
edges and the late one 134.

## Do the networks differ at all?

A permutation test reshuffles the sessions between the two phases and asks
whether the observed differences exceed those of the reshuffled data. Its
global statistics test the networks as a whole, so they need no correction
for the number of edges.

```{r permutation}
perm <- permutation_htna(grp, iter = 1000, seed = 1)
perm
```

The sum of the absolute edge differences, 2.76, is larger than in any of
the 1,000 reshuffles (p = 0.001), and the largest single difference, 0.181,
is exceeded in about one percent of them (p = 0.012). The way the
programmers and the agent interact did change between the two halves of
the study.

## Where in the actor structure?

The descriptive comparison splits the edge differences by actor-pair block;
differences are early minus late.

```{r compare}
cmp <- compare_htna(grp)
summary(cmp)
```

The four blocks change by similar amounts on average (mean absolute
differences between 0.016 and 0.022), so the change is not confined to one
kind of transition. The AI-to-AI block holds the largest single difference
(0.181). The transitions from AI codes to human codes carry more weight in
the late sessions (mean difference, early minus late, −0.006), and those
between AI codes carry less by the same amount: after an AI event, the next
event is more often a human one late in the study. The overall similarity of the two networks stays high.

```{r metrics}
head(as.data.frame(cmp, what = "metrics"), 8)
```

The edge weights correlate at 0.959 between the phases: the late network is
a modified version of the early one, not a different process.

## Which transitions differ?

The permutation test also gives a p-value for each of the 135 edges.

```{r edge-tests}
xtabs(~ sig, data = summary(perm))
```

At the 0.05 level, 31 edges differ. With 135 tests about seven would be
expected by chance alone, so the edge tests are repeated with the
Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment of the p-values.

```{r edge-tests-bh}
permutation_htna(grp, iter = 1000, adjust = "BH", seed = 1)
```

After the adjustment no edge remains significant. The difference
network shows the 31 unadjusted differences, green where the early
sessions have the larger weight and red where the late sessions do.

```{r edge-plot, fig.height = 6}
plot_htna_diff(perm)
```

The Bayesian comparison estimates the size of each difference with a
credible interval.

```{r bayes}
bc <- bayes_compare_htna(grp, draws = 5000, seed = 1)
xtabs(~ sig, data = summary(bc))
head(summary(bc))
```

Thirty-six edges have a 95% credible interval that excludes zero and pass
the default size thresholds; the Bayesian model treats every transition as
independent and makes no correction for multiplicity, so this count is an
upper bound on the edges that changed. The first rows of the table show the
pattern: an AI `Ask` is followed by an AI `Execute` with probability 0.033
in the early sessions and 0.012 in the late ones, and by a human
`Frustrate` with probability 0.099 and 0.131.

```{r bayes-plot, fig.height = 6}
plot_htna_diff(bc)
```

## Has the turn-taking changed?

Replacing every code by its actor type gives the meta-paths of the
sessions, and the sequence comparison asks which of them became more or
less frequent.

```{r meta-paths}
sequence_compare_htna(grp, level = "type", sub = 2:4, iter = 1000)
```

Runs in which the AI acts twice in a row after a human event
(Human $\to$ Human $\to$ AI $\to$ AI, Human $\to$ AI $\to$ AI) are more
frequent in the early sessions than independence predicts (positive
residuals), and strict alternation (Human $\to$ AI $\to$ Human,
Human $\to$ AI $\to$ Human $\to$ AI) is more frequent in the late sessions.
None of these patterns differs significantly after the false discovery rate
correction (smallest adjusted p = 0.084), so the shift towards shorter AI
turns is a tendency, not an established change.

## Conclusion

The networks of the early and late sessions differ as wholes (p = 0.001),
yet no single transition differs once the 135 tests are taken into
account, and the four actor-pair blocks change by similar amounts. The
change between the two halves of the study is diffuse: many transitions
shift a little, in the direction of more frequent alternation between the
programmer and the agent and fewer consecutive AI actions, rather than a
few transitions changing a lot. A report of this comparison should rest on
the global test and the actor-pair summary, and present the individual
edge differences as descriptive.

## When to use which

- `permutation_htna()`: whether two networks differ, globally and edge by
  edge, respecting the nesting of transitions in sessions; set `adjust` for
  the edge tests.
- `compare_htna()`: where the differences lie in the actor structure, and
  how similar the networks are overall; descriptive only.
- `bayes_compare_htna()`: how large each difference is and how precisely it
  is estimated.
- `sequence_compare_htna(level = "type")`: whether the turn-taking between
  the actors has changed, beyond single transitions.
